citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $P$ be a probability measure on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$. Here $L^2(P)$ is the real space of square-integrable measurable functions modulo equality $P$-almost surely, with its usual quotient norm ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]). For $f\in L^2(P)$, the integral $Pf:=\int f\,dP$ is finite and independent of the representative: Cauchy–Schwarz on the probability space gives $\int|f|\,dP\le\|f\|_2$, and the expectation of integrable representatives is invariant under almost-sure equality ([[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]], [[lem-expectation-is-independent-of-the-ae-representative]]).

Define the **mean-zero square-integrable space** by

$$L^2_0(P):=\{f\in L^2(P):Pf=0\}.$$

It carries the norm inherited from $L^2(P)$. Countable Choice is not needed for this definition; a later local Hilbert-space argument uses it only to inherit completeness from the library's general $L^2$ Hilbert-space result.

derivations.claim: The constant function $1$ belongs to $L^2(P)$ and has norm $1$, since $P(\mathcal X)=1$. For each $f\in L^2(P)$, the pairing in [F1] satisfies $Pf=\langle f,1\rangle_P$, so [F2] gives $|Pf|\le\|f\|_2$. Thus $f\mapsto Pf$ is a bounded linear functional, and its kernel is exactly $L^2_0(P)$ by [F3].

The kernel is linear. If $f_n\in L^2_0(P)$ and $f_n\to f$ in $L^2(P)$, then $|Pf|=|P(f-f_n)|\le\|f-f_n\|_2\to0$ by step 1.1 and linearity of the pairing [F1], so $f\in L^2_0(P)$. Hence the kernel is closed.

Every Cauchy sequence in $L^2_0(P)$ is Cauchy in $L^2(P)$, which is complete by [F1] under the Countable Choice assumption [A1]; its $L^2(P)$ limit lies in $L^2_0(P)$ by step 2.1. The restricted inner product is therefore complete, proving the asserted Hilbert-space property.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mu$ be a positive measure and let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
If in addition $|
u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Put $q=\sqrt p$, $q_t=\sqrt{p_t}$, and $r_t=q_t-q-(t/2)sq$. By [F1], $\|r_t\|_2=o(t)$, while [F2] gives $\|q\|_2^2=\int p\,d\mu=1$ and $\|q_t\|_2^2=\int p_t\,d\mu=1$.
If $s'$ is another score with remainder $r'_t=o_{L^2}(t)$, subtracting its expansion from [F1] gives $\|(t/2)(s-s')q\|_2\le\|r_t\|_2+\|r'_t\|_2=o(t)$.

Set $u_t=(t/2)sq+r_t$. Since $\|sq\|_2^2=\int s^2p\,d\mu=Ps^2<\infty$, we have $\|u_t\|_2=O(t)$ and $q_t=q+u_t$. The products $q r_t$ and $u_t^2$ are integrable by [F3]. Pointwise expansion and linearity [F4] give $0=\int(q+u_t)^2d\mu-\int q^2d\mu=t\,Ps+2\int q r_t\,d\mu+\|u_t\|_2^2$. By [F3], $|\int q r_t\,d\mu|\le\|q\|_2\|r_t\|_2=o(t)$ and $\|u_t\|_2^2=O(t^2)=o(t)$. Dividing by $t>0$ and taking $t\downarrow0$ gives $Ps=0$.
Divide by $t/2$ and let $t\downarrow0$. Then $\|(s-s')q\|_2^2=P[(s-s')^2]=0$, so $s=s'$ as an element of $L^2(P)$. Together with step 2.1 this proves mean zero and uniqueness.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) so that $L^2_0(P)$ is the real Hilbert space established by [[thm-mean-zero-square-integrable-space-is-hilbert]]. For a tangent set $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)\subseteq L^2_0(P)$, its **linear span** is the set of all finite real linear combinations of elements of $\dot{\mathcal M}(P)$; the span of the empty set is $\{0\}$. Its **tangent space** $\mathcal T(P)$ is the closure of that span in the $L^2(P)$ norm. The closure consists of limits of sequences from the span, equivalently of points every positive-radius norm ball around which meets the span.

The tangent set itself is retained separately and may be a cone rather than a vector space.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). For any probability measure $P$, the space $L^2_0(P)$ of [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]] is a closed real linear subspace of real $L^2(P)$ with pairing $\langle f,g\rangle_P:=\int fg\,dP$; consequently it is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). The only choice use is the Countable Choice assumption already required by the general $L^2(P)$ completeness supplier.

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ ([[def-vector-space]]). A subset
$W \subseteq V$ is a **linear subspace** of $V$ when

- **(W1)** $0_V \in W$;
- **(W2)** $W$ is closed under the vector addition: $u, v \in W$ implies
  $u + v \in W$;
- **(W3)** $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication: $\lambda \in F$ and
  $v \in W$ imply $\lambda v \in W$.

Every vector space $V$ has the two **trivial linear subspaces** $\{0_V\}$ and $V$
itself; a linear subspace $W$ with $W \ne V$ is called **proper**.

**The restricted operations are the required data, and $W$ is a vector space.**
By (W2) the vector addition of $V$ restricts to a binary operation
$W \times W \to W$, and by (W3) the scalar multiplication restricts to a map
$F \times W \to W$. With these and the element $0_V$, the set $W$ is a vector
space over $F$:

- axioms (V2)–(V5) are equations required of elements of $W$, which are in
  particular elements of $V$, so they are inherited from $V$; likewise
  associativity and commutativity of the restricted addition;
- $0_V$ lies in $W$ by (W1) and is a two-sided identity for the restricted
  addition, since it is one in $V$;
- for $v \in W$ the vector $(-1_F)v$ lies in $W$ by (W3), and
  $(-1_F)v = -v$ ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]), so $-v \in W$
  and $v + (-v) = 0_V$ holds in $W$.

So $(W,+,0_V)$ is an abelian group, which is axiom (V1), and $W$ is a vector
space over $F$ **whose zero vector and whose additive inverses are those of
$V$**. In the language of [[def-subgroup]], the three displayed conditions
(S1) $0_V \in W$, (S2) closure under addition and (S3) closure under additive
inverses all hold, so $W$ is a subgroup of the abelian group $(V,+,0_V)$
([[def-group]]); that reading, and its converse, are recorded as
[[lem-linear-subspace-is-a-subgroup]] and are cited from there rather than
re-argued below.

If $x\notin\overline V$, some $r>0$ has $B(x,r)\cap V=\varnothing$. For any $y$ with $\|y-x\|_2<r/2$, the triangle inequality gives $B(y,r/2)\subset B(x,r)$, so $y\notin\overline V$. Hence the complement of $\overline V$ is open and $\overline V$ is closed.

Write $\overline V=\mathcal T(P)$. If $x,y\in\overline V$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose $u,v\in V$ with $\|x-u\|_2<\varepsilon/2$ and $\|y-v\|_2<\varepsilon/2$. Then $u+v\in V$ and $\|(x+y)-(u+v)\|_2<\varepsilon$, so $x+y\in\overline V$. For $a\in\mathbb R$, if $a=0$ then $ax=0\in V$; if $a\ne0$, choose $u\in V$ with $\|x-u\|_2<\varepsilon/|a|$, giving $au\in V$ and $\|ax-au\|_2<\varepsilon$. Thus $\overline V$ is linear.

A Cauchy sequence in $\overline V$ converges in $L^2_0(P)$ by [F2] under [A1]. Since $\overline V$ is closed by step 1.2, that limit lies in $\overline V$. Therefore the tangent space is complete as well as a closed linear subspace, as asserted.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\mathcal M$ be a model of probability measures on a measurable space $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let $\epsilon>0$, and let $t\mapsto P_t\in\mathcal M$ be a path for $0\le t<\epsilon$ with $P_0=P$. It is **dominated by a common measure** when one supplied sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$ satisfies $P_t\ll\mu$ for every $t$ ([[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]). Write $p_t=dP_t/d\mu$ and $p=p_0$ for simultaneously supplied nonnegative density versions; the existence and normalization of each density are the Radon–Nikodym properties in [[def-likelihood-density]] and [[thm-radon-nikodym-density-exists-and-is-unique-up-to-almost-everywhere-equality]]. The Axiom of Choice is the library convention for selecting such a family of versions along a path ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The DQM property below is unchanged by replacing any $p_t$ by another version, since each $L^2(\mu)$ norm is unchanged by a $\mu$-null modification.

The path is **differentiable in quadratic mean at $0$**, with **score** $s\in L^2(P)$, when

$$\left\|\sqrt{p_t}-\sqrt p-\frac{t}{2}s\sqrt p\right\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(t)\qquad(t\downarrow0).$$

Here $o(t)$ means that the displayed norm divided by $t$ tends to $0$ as $t\downarrow0$; $L^2(P)$ and $L^2(\mu)$ are quotient spaces modulo almost-everywhere equality ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). The definition is directional. A two-sided regular submodel qualifies by restricting it to $t\ge0$. No mean-zero condition is assumed in this definition.

Assume the density-version convention for the path in [[def-dqm-submodel-through-a-law]]. If $s\in L^2(P)$ is a DQM score, then $Ps=0$, so $s\in L^2_0(P)$ ([[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]). Moreover, any two scores satisfying the same DQM expansion agree $P$-almost surely. The normalization argument itself uses no choice beyond the density versions already supplied in the definition.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $X$ be a set. A **sigma-algebra on $X$** is an algebra of subsets
$\mathcal A$ ([[def-algebra-of-subsets]]) that is closed under countable unions:
whenever $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ is a sequence in $\mathcal A$,

$$\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}A_n\in\mathcal A.$$

The pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ then has a fixed ambient set $X$. Complements in the
sigma-algebra axioms always mean complements relative to that $X$.

A **measurable space** is a pair $(X,\mathcal A)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a
sigma-algebra $\mathcal A$ on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). The members of
$\mathcal A$ are the **measurable subsets** of $X$.

Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].
For every set $X$, the counting set function $\#_X$ of [[def-counting-measure]] is a measure on $(X,\mathcal P(X))$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

For $a>0$, the function $x\mapsto a^x$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$ and
$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with
$$(x^\alpha)'=\alpha x^{\alpha-1}.$$

Its only null set is empty, so each $P_t$ is absolutely continuous with respect to it. Direct calculation gives $Ps=p(1/p)+(1-p)(-1/(1-p))=0$ and $Ps^2=p/p^2+(1-p)/(1-p)^2=1/[p(1-p)]<\infty$. Hence the score is in $L^2_0(P)$ and has the stated variance.

derivations.claim: Every subset of $\{-1,+1\}$ and its complement lie in the full power set, and every countable union of such subsets is still a subset; thus the power set is a sigma-algebra by [F4], and with this sigma-algebra the sample set is a measurable space by [F4]. Counting measure on the two-point set is a measure of total mass two by [F5, F6], hence sigma-finite by the constant sequence of covers $E_n=\{-1,+1\}$; its only null set is empty. For every $\theta\in[0,1]$, the masses $(1+\theta)/2$ and $(1-\theta)/2$ are nonnegative and sum to one, so $P_\theta$ is a probability measure dominated by counting measure. At $\theta=0$ both masses are $1/2$, so $\sqrt{p_0(x)}=1/\sqrt2$.
If a one-sided DQM path has score $s$, [F1] on each atom gives $\sqrt{P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}}=1/\sqrt2+t s(x)/(2\sqrt2)+o(t)$. Squaring each expansion yields $P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}=1/2+t s(x)/2+o(t)$.

Conversely, for each $a\ge0$, take $\theta(t)=at$ for sufficiently small $t\ge0$. Then $P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}=(1+atx)/2$, and [F7] at $1/2$ gives $\sqrt{P_{\theta(t)}\{x\}}=1/\sqrt2+t ax/(2\sqrt2)+o(t)$ on each atom. The two-coordinate counting-measure $L^2$ remainder is $o(t)$, so this path has score $aX$. Its densities are explicit, so [A1] requires no selection in this construction. Thus every vector on the nonnegative ray is an allowed score.

Subtract the two mass expansions from step 2.1. Since $\theta(t)=P_{\theta(t)}\{+1\}-P_{\theta(t)}\{-1\}$, we get $\theta(t)/t\to(s(+1)-s(-1))/2$. By [F2], $P_0s=(s(+1)+s(-1))/2=0$, so this limit equals $s(+1)$. The constraints $\theta(t)\ge0$ and $t>0$ force the limit $a:=s(+1)$ to be nonnegative, and $s(-1)=-a$; hence every score is $s(x)=ax$ with $a\ge0$.

The real span of $\{aX:a\ge0\}$ is $\{bX:b\in\mathbb R\}$, and every mean-zero function on the equiprobable two-point space has values $(b,-b)$, so this span is $L^2_0(P_0)$. This space is closed in $L^2(P_0)$ by [F8], hence its closure—and therefore the tangent space by [F3]—is $L^2_0(P_0)$. It strictly contains the non-linear score cone because $X$ is in the cone but $-X$ is not.
